messages.author: 67a95d8c18d98837
messages.subject: show alternate axis text
parts:
Hi,

there is a way to show alternate axis text?

I've a bar charts plot, but the text of x axis is too small.

If I increase the size the text overlap. It's possible to show
alternate axis text?

thanks,

Alfredo

messages.author: 67a95d8c18d98837
messages.subject: Re: show alternate axis text
parts:
a little example:

library(ggplot2)

a <- seq(1,100)

b <- rnorm(100,5)

data <- as.data.frame(cbind(a,b))

p <- ggplot(data,aes(factor(a),b))

p + geom_bar() + opts(scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0,100,by=5)))

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: show alternate axis text
parts:
Hi:

Here's another way to get the plot using geom_segment() in place of geom_bar():

a <- 1L:100L
b <- rnorm(100,5)
dat <- data.frame(a, b)
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(a, b))
p + geom_segment(aes(xend = a, yend = 0), size = 1) +
scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0,100,by=5))

To get the thickness of the original bar chart, use size = 2 instead.

However, this is not a particularly good data display because the bars
distract from the actual behavior of the series. A better time series
plot, if for no reason other than the use of (far) less ink, is

p + geom_point() + geom_line() + ylim(0, 8) +
scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0,100,by=5))

The two graphs have the same x and y scale and convey the same
information, but the line plot version provides a better sense of how
the observations behave over time. Google 'ink to information ratio'
for a tutorial on the graphical principles behind this statement
(leaving aside the perceptual psychology issues that are also relevant
to the discussion).

HTH,
Dennis

messages.author: 22aafb2aa2902d9d
messages.subject: Re: show alternate axis text
parts:
I think what you were trying to do is achieved with (after running the
example code you provided)

p + geom_bar() + scale_x_discrete(breaks = seq(0,100,by=5))

However I agree with Dennis that a bar plot is not be the best way of
displaying the data. If you've actually got that many points in your
real dataset you'll probably find it looks a lot clearer using points,
or lines if the data is related along a time or other series.

Samuel
